sets.title: The heart in the chest and its wall

labels.name: Trachea
labels.fn: The windpipe: a tube held open by rings of stiff tissue that carries air between the throat and the lungs. It runs down the chest just in front of the esophagus and above the heart.

labels.name: Thymus
labels.fn: A soft organ in the upper chest, in front of the large vessels leaving the heart. It is large in children and shrinks after puberty, when much of it is replaced by fat.

labels.name: Base
labels.fn: The broad upper end of the heart, where the large vessels enter and leave. Despite the name it is at the top: the heart sits upside down compared with a jar standing on its base.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped sheet of muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity. The heart rests on its upper surface, tilted so the apex points down and to your left.

labels.name: Esophagus
labels.fn: The muscular tube that carries swallowed food from the throat to the stomach. It runs through the mediastinum behind the heart and the trachea.

labels.name: Mediastinum
labels.fn: The central compartment of the thoracic cavity, between the two lungs. It holds the heart inside its pericardial sac, the large vessels, the trachea, the esophagus and the thymus.

labels.name: Right lung
labels.fn: The organ where blood takes up oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide. The right lung is slightly larger than the left, because the heart bulges into the left side of the chest.

labels.name: Left lung
labels.fn: The organ where blood takes up oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide. The left lung is a little smaller than the right and has a notch that makes room for the heart, which sits more to the left.

labels.name: Pericardial cavity
labels.fn: The thin space between the two layers of serous pericardium. A few milliliters of serous fluid in it let the heart slide as it beats; if fluid or blood fills it quickly, the heart cannot expand (cardiac tamponade).

follow.q: A stab wound lets blood collect quickly between the layers of the serous pericardium. Why does the heart pump less blood?
options: The stiff fibrous pericardium cannot stretch, so the trapped blood squeezes the heart and it cannot fill between beats
The blood dilutes the serous fluid, so the heart loses its lubrication and stops
The blood clots onto the myocardium and paralyzes it
The pericardial cavity is connected to the pleural cavity, so the lungs collapse
follow.why: The fibrous pericardium is tough and barely stretches. Blood that builds up quickly in the pericardial cavity has nowhere to go, so pressure around the heart rises and the heart cannot expand to fill. Less filling means less blood pumped out with each beat. This is cardiac tamponade.

labels.name: Apex of heart
labels.fn: The pointed lower tip of the heart. It points down, forward and to your left and rests on the diaphragm, which is why the strongest heartbeat is felt on the left side of the chest.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped sheet of muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity. The heart rests on its upper surface, tilted so the apex points down and to your left.

labels.name: Edge of parietal pericardium (cut)
labels.fn: The cut edge of the pericardial sac that encloses the heart: a tough outer fibrous layer lined by the parietal layer of serous pericardium. It anchors the heart in the mediastinum and keeps it from overfilling.

labels.name: Pericardial cavity

labels.name: Endocardium
labels.fn: The thin inner lining of the heart's chambers and valves: a simple squamous endothelium on a thin layer of connective tissue. Its smooth surface lets blood flow without sticking.

labels.name: Fibrous pericardium
labels.fn: The tough outer layer of the pericardial sac, made of dense connective tissue. It anchors the heart to the diaphragm and nearby structures and, because it barely stretches, keeps the heart from overfilling.

follow.q: Which layer is the outermost covering of the heart?
follow.why: From outside in: fibrous pericardium, then the parietal layer of serous pericardium, the pericardial cavity, the epicardium (the visceral layer, stuck to the heart), the myocardium and the endocardium. The fibrous layer is outermost, which is why it can anchor the heart to its surroundings.

labels.name: Myocardium
labels.fn: The thick middle layer of the heart wall, made of cardiac muscle. Its contraction does the pumping, so it is thickest where the heart must push hardest.

follow.q: Which layer of the heart wall does the actual pumping?
follow.why: Only the myocardium is made of cardiac muscle, and only muscle can shorten and squeeze. The endocardium and epicardium are thin linings, and the fibrous pericardium is connective tissue that holds the heart in place.

labels.name: Parietal layer of serous pericardium
labels.fn: The serous membrane that lines the inside of the fibrous pericardium. It secretes serous fluid into the pericardial cavity and faces the epicardium across that thin space.

labels.name: Epicardium (visceral layer of serous pericardium)
labels.fn: The visceral layer of the serous pericardium: a thin serous membrane stuck to the outer surface of the heart, forming the heart wall's outermost layer. It faces the parietal layer across the pericardial cavity.

labels.name: Superior vena cava
labels.fn: The large vein that returns blood from the head, neck, arms and chest to the right atrium, entering it from above.

follow.q: Blood from your right arm reaches the heart through which vessel?
follow.why: Veins above the diaphragm, including those of the arms, head and neck, drain into the superior vena cava, which opens into the right atrium. The inferior vena cava drains the body below the diaphragm.

labels.name: Right pulmonary artery
labels.fn: The branch of the pulmonary trunk that carries blood to the right lung. It is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart, even though that blood is low in oxygen.

labels.name: Left pulmonary artery
labels.fn: The branch of the pulmonary trunk that carries blood to the left lung. It is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart, even though that blood is low in oxygen.

follow.q: What makes a pulmonary artery an artery?
options: It carries blood away from the heart
It carries blood rich in oxygen
It has valves along its length
It carries blood at low pressure
follow.why: Arteries and veins are named by direction, not by oxygen. The pulmonary arteries carry blood away from the heart to the lungs; that blood is low in oxygen, which is why "arteries carry blood high in oxygen" is not a safe rule.

labels.name: Left pulmonary veins
labels.fn: The veins that return blood from the left lung to the left atrium. They are veins because they carry blood toward the heart, and the blood in them has just picked up oxygen in the lung.

follow.q: Where do the pulmonary veins empty?
follow.why: The pulmonary veins bring blood back from the lungs into the left atrium, which passes it to the left ventricle to be pumped to the body.

labels.name: Pulmonary trunk
labels.fn: The short, wide vessel that leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve and splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries. It carries blood to the lungs.

follow.q: Which chamber pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk?
follow.why: The pulmonary valve sits between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk. The left ventricle pumps into the aorta, and the atria pump only into the ventricles.

labels.name: Right pulmonary veins
labels.fn: The veins that return blood from the right lung to the left atrium. They are veins because they carry blood toward the heart, and the blood in them has just picked up oxygen in the lung.

labels.name: Auricle of left atrium
labels.fn: The ear-shaped pouch on the front of the left atrium. It adds a little extra room to the atrium, letting it hold more blood before the blood moves on to the ventricle.

labels.name: Right atrium
labels.fn: The upper right chamber. It receives blood returning from the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae, plus the heart's own used blood, and passes it through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle.

follow.q: Which vessels empty into the right atrium?

The left and right pulmonary arteries
follow.why: The venae cavae carry blood back from the body and open into the right atrium. The pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium, and the pulmonary trunk and aorta leave the ventricles.

labels.name: Left ventricle
labels.fn: The lower left chamber and the heart's main pump. It pushes blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and on to the whole body, which takes high pressure, so its wall is the thickest in the heart.

follow.q: For years, the pressure in a person's body arteries has been well above normal. Which chamber's wall thickens most?
follow.why: The left ventricle must raise its pressure above the pressure in the aorta before its valve opens. Higher arterial pressure means more work every beat, and muscle that works harder grows thicker.

labels.name: Right ventricle
labels.fn: The lower right chamber. It pumps blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and on to the lungs. The lungs are close and offer little resistance, so its wall is much thinner than the left ventricle's.

follow.q: Why is the right ventricle's wall thinner than the left ventricle's?
options: It pumps blood only to the nearby lungs, which need a much lower pressure than the whole body
It pumps less blood per beat than the left ventricle
It receives blood that has less oxygen, so its muscle is weaker
Its wall is thinned by the pressure of the lungs pressing on it
follow.why: Both ventricles pump the same volume per beat. The difference is pressure: pushing blood through the short, low-resistance route to the lungs takes far less pressure than pushing it through the whole body, so the right ventricle builds less muscle.

labels.fn: The left atrioventricular valve, also called the bicuspid valve for its two cusps. It lets blood move from the left atrium into the left ventricle and shuts when the ventricle contracts, stopping backflow into the atrium.

follow.q: The mitral valve fails to close fully. Where does blood leak when the left ventricle contracts?
follow.why: The mitral valve guards the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle. If it leaks, the rising pressure in the contracting ventricle pushes some blood backward through that opening into the left atrium.

labels.name: Right atrium
labels.fn: The upper right chamber. It receives blood returning from the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae, plus the heart's own used blood, and passes it through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle.

follow.q: Which vessels empty into the right atrium?
options: The superior and inferior venae cavae
The left and right pulmonary arteries
follow.why: The venae cavae carry blood back from the body and open into the right atrium. The pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium, and the pulmonary trunk and aorta leave the ventricles.

labels.name: Left ventricle
labels.fn: The lower left chamber and the heart's main pump. It pushes blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and on to the whole body, which takes high pressure, so its wall is the thickest in the heart.

follow.q: For years, the pressure in a person's body arteries has been well above normal. Which chamber's wall thickens most?
follow.why: The left ventricle must raise its pressure above the pressure in the aorta before its valve opens. Higher arterial pressure means more work every beat, and muscle that works harder grows thicker.

labels.name: Tricuspid valve
labels.fn: The right atrioventricular valve, with three cusps. It lets blood move from the right atrium into the right ventricle and shuts when the ventricle contracts, so blood cannot flow back into the atrium.

follow.q: What closes the tricuspid valve?
options: Pressure in the right ventricle rising above pressure in the right atrium
The papillary muscles pulling the cusps shut
A nerve signal that tightens the valve ring
follow.why: Valves are passive flaps. When the ventricle contracts its pressure climbs above the atrium's, and blood pushing backward swings the cusps together. The papillary muscles and chordae only keep the closed cusps from flipping up into the atrium.

labels.name: Right ventricle
labels.fn: The lower right chamber. It pumps blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and on to the lungs. The lungs are close and offer little resistance, so its wall is much thinner than the left ventricle's.

follow.q: Why is the right ventricle's wall thinner than the left ventricle's?
options: It pumps blood only to the nearby lungs, which need a much lower pressure than the whole body
It pumps less blood per beat than the left ventricle
It receives blood that has less oxygen, so its muscle is weaker
Its wall is thinned by the pressure of the lungs pressing on it
follow.why: Both ventricles pump the same volume per beat. The difference is pressure: pushing blood through the short, low-resistance route to the lungs takes far less pressure than pushing it through the whole body, so the right ventricle builds less muscle.

labels.name: Inferior vena cava
labels.fn: The largest vein in the body. It returns blood from everything below the diaphragm (legs, abdomen and pelvis) to the right atrium, entering it from below.

labels.name: Systemic veins from upper body
labels.fn: Veins that collect deoxygenated blood from the head, neck and arms and lead it to the superior vena cava.

labels.name: Systemic capillaries of upper body
labels.fn: Capillary beds in the tissues of the head, neck and arms. Here blood gives oxygen and nutrients to the cells and picks up carbon dioxide, turning deoxygenated.

follow.q: What happens to blood as it passes through systemic capillaries?
options: It gives off oxygen and picks up carbon dioxide
It picks up oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide
It is pumped to a higher pressure
It collects into the pulmonary veins
follow.why: Cells use oxygen and make carbon dioxide, so each gas moves down its concentration gradient: oxygen out of the blood into the tissues, carbon dioxide from the tissues into the blood. The reverse happens in the pulmonary capillaries.

labels.name: Systemic arteries to upper body
labels.fn: Branches of the aorta that carry oxygenated blood to the head, neck and arms, the upper part of the systemic circuit.

labels.name: Pulmonary capillaries in lungs
labels.fn: The tiny vessels around the lungs' air sacs, where the pulmonary circuit does its work: blood gives off carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen, turning from deoxygenated to oxygenated.

follow.q: Blood leaving the pulmonary capillaries goes next to which chamber?
follow.why: From the pulmonary capillaries, oxygenated blood collects into the pulmonary veins, which empty into the left atrium.

labels.name: Pulmonary trunk
labels.fn: The short, wide vessel that leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve and splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries. It carries blood to the lungs.

follow.q: Which chamber pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk?
follow.why: The pulmonary valve sits between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk. The left ventricle pumps into the aorta, and the atria pump only into the ventricles.

The left and right pulmonary arteries

labels.name: Left atrium
labels.fn: The upper left chamber. It receives blood returning from the lungs through the four pulmonary veins and passes it through the mitral valve to the left ventricle.

follow.q: Blood entering the left atrium has just come from where?
options: The lungs, through the pulmonary veins
The body, through the venae cavae
The right atrium, through the interatrial septum
The left ventricle, through the mitral valve
follow.why: The pulmonary veins drain the lungs into the left atrium. After birth the interatrial septum is closed, and the mitral valve lets blood move only from atrium to ventricle, never back.

labels.name: Systemic veins from lower body
labels.fn: Veins that collect deoxygenated blood from the abdomen, pelvis and legs and lead it to the inferior vena cava.

labels.name: Systemic arteries to lower body
labels.fn: The continuation of the aorta and its branches carrying oxygenated blood to the abdomen, pelvis and legs, the lower part of the systemic circuit.

labels.name: Systemic capillaries of lower body
labels.fn: Capillary beds in the tissues of the abdomen, pelvis and legs, where blood unloads oxygen and nutrients to the cells and picks up carbon dioxide and wastes.

labels.name: Left coronary artery
labels.fn: The first branch of the aorta on the left. After a short course it splits into the anterior interventricular artery and the circumflex artery, which together supply most of the left ventricle.

labels.name: Right coronary artery

options: The base of the aorta, just past the aortic valve
follow.why: The coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, leaving it just beyond the aortic valve. They fill mainly when the ventricles relax (diastole), when the heart muscle is not squeezing them shut.

labels.name: Circumflex artery
labels.fn: The branch of the left coronary artery that curves around the left side of the heart in the groove between the left atrium and left ventricle. It supplies the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle.

labels.name: Anterior interventricular artery
labels.fn: The branch of the left coronary artery that runs down the front of the heart between the two ventricles (also called the left anterior descending artery). It supplies the front of both ventricles and much of the interventricular septum.

follow.q: A clot blocks the anterior interventricular artery. Which region is most likely to be damaged?
options: The front of the left ventricle and the interventricular septum
The back of the right ventricle
follow.why: This artery runs down the front groove between the ventricles and feeds the front wall of the left ventricle and most of the septum. Muscle downstream of a blocked artery loses its oxygen supply (ischemia) and can die (a myocardial infarction).

labels.name: Atrial arteries
labels.fn: Small branches of the coronary arteries that supply the walls of the atria.

labels.name: Anterior cardiac veins
labels.fn: Small veins on the front of the right ventricle that empty straight into the right atrium instead of into the coronary sinus.

labels.name: Great cardiac vein
labels.fn: The vein that runs up the front of the heart beside the anterior interventricular artery, collecting deoxygenated blood from the front of the ventricles and carrying it into the coronary sinus.

labels.name: Small cardiac vein
labels.fn: A vein along the lower right edge of the heart that drains the right side and empties into the coronary sinus.

labels.name: Marginal artery
labels.fn: A branch of the right coronary artery that runs along the lower right edge of the heart and supplies the right ventricle.

labels.name: Coronary sinus
labels.fn: A wide vein in the groove on the back of the heart between the atria and ventricles. It gathers blood from most of the cardiac veins and empties it into the right atrium.

follow.q: Where does the coronary sinus empty?
follow.why: The heart's own used, deoxygenated blood collects in the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium beside the inferior vena cava. From there it joins the rest of the body's returning blood.

labels.name: Small cardiac vein
labels.fn: A vein along the lower right edge of the heart that drains the right side and empties into the coronary sinus.

labels.name: Circumflex artery
labels.fn: The branch of the left coronary artery that curves around the left side of the heart in the groove between the left atrium and left ventricle. It supplies the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle.

labels.name: Great cardiac vein
labels.fn: The vein that runs up the front of the heart beside the anterior interventricular artery, collecting deoxygenated blood from the front of the ventricles and carrying it into the coronary sinus.

labels.name: Marginal artery
labels.fn: A branch of the right coronary artery that runs along the lower right edge of the heart and supplies the right ventricle.

labels.name: Posterior interventricular artery
labels.fn: The artery that runs down the back of the heart between the ventricles, usually from the right coronary artery. It supplies the back of both ventricles and it meets branches of the anterior interventricular artery near the apex (an anastomosis).

labels.name: Posterior cardiac vein
labels.fn: A vein on the back of the left ventricle that drains it into the coronary sinus.

labels.name: Left ventricle

labels.name: Middle cardiac vein

labels.name: Marginal artery
labels.fn: A branch of the right coronary artery that runs along the lower right edge of the heart and supplies the right ventricle.

labels.fn: A branch of each subclavian artery that climbs through the neck bones to the base of the brain, where the two join to form the basilar artery.

labels.name: Right common carotid
labels.fn: The artery up the right side of the neck, from the brachiocephalic trunk. At the level of the upper neck it splits into the internal carotid (brain) and external carotid (face and scalp) arteries.

labels.name: Right subclavian
labels.fn: The artery to the right arm, from the brachiocephalic trunk. It passes under the collarbone and becomes the axillary artery in the armpit; it also gives off the right vertebral artery.

labels.name: Left common carotid
labels.fn: The artery up the left side of the neck, branching straight from the aortic arch. It splits into the internal carotid artery to the brain and the external carotid artery to the face and scalp.

options: At the side of the neck, beside the windpipe
On the inner wrist below the thumb
follow.why: The common carotid arteries run up either side of the neck next to the trachea, close to the skin, so each heartbeat's pressure wave can be felt there. The wrist, groin and knee sites are the radial, femoral and popliteal pulses.

labels.name: Left subclavian
labels.fn: The artery to the left arm, the last branch of the aortic arch. It passes under the collarbone, gives off the left vertebral artery and becomes the axillary artery.

labels.name: Brachiocephalic trunk
labels.fn: The first branch of the aortic arch, on the right. It is short and splits into the right common carotid artery (to the head) and the right subclavian artery (to the right arm). There is no left brachiocephalic trunk.

labels.name: Axillary
labels.fn: The continuation of the subclavian artery through the armpit (the axilla). At the arm it becomes the brachial artery.

labels.name: Aortic arch
labels.fn: The curve of the aorta above the heart, turning back and to the left. Its three branches supply the head and arms: the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery and the left subclavian artery.

follow.q: Which vessel is NOT a branch of the aortic arch?
follow.why: On the right side the arch gives one trunk, the brachiocephalic trunk, which then splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. The left common carotid and left subclavian leave the arch directly, so only the left carotid is a direct branch.

labels.name: Pulmonary trunk
labels.fn: The short, wide vessel that leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve and splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries. It carries blood to the lungs.

follow.q: Which chamber pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk?

labels.name: Ascending aorta
labels.fn: The first part of the aorta, rising from the left ventricle. Its only branches are the right and left coronary arteries.

labels.name: Descending aorta
labels.fn: The long part of the aorta that runs down behind the heart and through the diaphragm. Above the diaphragm it is the thoracic aorta; below it, the abdominal aorta.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped muscle between the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities. The descending aorta passes behind it through an opening called the aortic hiatus; above that point it is the thoracic aorta, below it the abdominal aorta.

labels.name: Celiac trunk
labels.fn: The first unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta, just below the diaphragm. It quickly splits to supply the stomach, liver, spleen and part of the pancreas.

labels.name: Renal
labels.fn: A paired branch of the abdominal aorta to each kidney. The kidneys receive about a fifth of the heart's output at rest, so these are short, wide arteries.

labels.name: Brachial
labels.fn: The main artery of the upper arm, continuing from the axillary artery. It runs along the inner arm and is where blood pressure is measured with a cuff; at the elbow it splits into the radial and ulnar arteries.

follow.q: Blood pressure cuffs are placed on the upper arm because they compress which artery?
follow.why: The brachial artery runs close to the skin along the inner upper arm, at about the level of the heart, so a cuff can squeeze it shut and a stethoscope at the elbow can hear flow return.

labels.name: Superior mesenteric
labels.fn: An unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta just below the celiac trunk. It supplies most of the gut below the stomach: the long, narrow part where most food is absorbed and the first half of the wider part that follows.

labels.name: Gonadal
labels.fn: A paired, slender branch of the abdominal aorta to the testes or ovaries (the testicular or ovarian artery).

labels.name: Inferior mesenteric
labels.fn: The lowest unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta. It supplies the last part of the gut, down to the end of the tract in the pelvis.

labels.name: Radial
labels.fn: The forearm artery on the thumb side, from the brachial artery. At the wrist it lies just under the skin over the bone, where the radial pulse is taken.

labels.name: Common iliac
labels.fn: One of the two terminal branches of the abdominal aorta. Each splits into an internal iliac artery to the pelvis and an external iliac artery to the leg.

labels.name: Ulnar
labels.fn: The forearm artery on the little-finger side, from the brachial artery. It joins the radial artery in the palm through the palmar arches.

labels.name: Internal iliac
labels.fn: The branch of the common iliac artery that supplies the pelvic organs, the buttocks and the inner thigh.

labels.name: External iliac
labels.fn: The branch of the common iliac artery headed to the leg. It passes under the ligament in the groin and becomes the femoral artery.

labels.name: Palmar arches
labels.fn: Arching connections between the radial and ulnar arteries in the palm. Because blood can reach the fingers from either artery, the hand keeps its supply if one of them is blocked.

labels.name: Deep femoral
labels.fn: The large branch of the femoral artery that runs deep in the thigh and supplies the thigh muscles and the femur.

labels.name: Femoral
labels.fn: The main artery of the thigh, continuing from the external iliac artery. In the groin it lies close to the skin, where the femoral pulse is felt and where catheters are often inserted.

labels.name: Descending genicular
labels.fn: A small branch of the femoral artery that runs down to the inner side of the knee and helps supply the knee joint.

labels.name: Popliteal
labels.fn: The continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee, where the popliteal pulse is felt. Below the knee it splits into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.

labels.name: Posterior tibial
labels.fn: The branch of the popliteal artery down the back of the leg. It passes behind the bump on the inner ankle, where its pulse is felt, and continues into the sole of the foot.

labels.name: Anterior tibial
labels.fn: The branch of the popliteal artery to the front of the leg. At the ankle it becomes the dorsalis pedis artery on top of the foot.

labels.name: Fibular
labels.fn: A branch of the posterior tibial artery that runs down the outer side of the leg and supplies the muscles there (also called the peroneal artery).

labels.name: Dorsalis pedis
labels.fn: The continuation of the anterior tibial artery on the top of the foot, where the pedal pulse is felt. Checking it tells you blood is reaching the end of the leg.

labels.name: Plantar arch
labels.fn: The arching artery in the sole of the foot, fed by the posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries. It supplies the toes from two directions.

labels.name: Left common carotid artery

labels.name: Abdominal aorta
labels.fn: The descending aorta below the diaphragm. It gives off the celiac trunk, the mesenteric, renal and gonadal arteries, and ends by splitting into the two common iliac arteries.

follow.q: The abdominal aorta ends by dividing into which pair of arteries?
follow.why: At about the level of the navel the abdominal aorta splits into the right and left common iliac arteries. Each then divides into an internal iliac (pelvis) and an external iliac, which becomes the femoral artery in the thigh.

labels.name: Anterior communicating
labels.fn: A short link between the two anterior cerebral arteries at the front of the cerebral arterial circle. It lets blood cross from one side to the other.

labels.name: Middle cerebral
labels.fn: The largest branch of the internal carotid artery. It runs out to the side of the brain and supplies most of its outer surface, which is why blockage of this artery is the most common cause of a stroke.

labels.name: Anterior cerebral
labels.fn: A branch of the internal carotid artery that runs forward and up between the two halves of the brain, supplying their inner surfaces.

labels.name: Ophthalmic
labels.fn: A branch of the internal carotid artery that supplies the eye and the structures around it.

labels.name: Posterior communicating
labels.fn: A short link on each side of the cerebral arterial circle between the internal carotid and posterior cerebral arteries. It connects the front and back blood supplies of the brain.

follow.q: Why does a slowly narrowing internal carotid artery often cause no symptoms at first?

The brain can store enough oxygen for weeks
The external carotid artery takes over supplying the brain directly
The vertebral arteries grow larger within days
follow.why: The communicating arteries join the carotid and basilar supplies into a ring. If one input narrows slowly, blood can flow around the ring from the others. This is an anastomosis; it cannot help if the blockage is sudden and downstream of the circle.

labels.name: Posterior cerebral

labels.name: Internal carotid

labels.name: Basilar

labels.name: Vertebral

labels.fn: A paired branch of the abdominal aorta to each kidney. The kidneys receive about a fifth of the heart's output at rest, so these are short, wide arteries.

labels.name: Gonadal
labels.fn: A paired, slender branch of the abdominal aorta to the testes or ovaries (the testicular or ovarian artery).

labels.name: Superior mesenteric
labels.fn: An unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta just below the celiac trunk. It supplies most of the gut below the stomach: the long, narrow part where most food is absorbed and the first half of the wider part that follows.

labels.name: Abdominal aorta
labels.fn: The descending aorta below the diaphragm. It gives off the celiac trunk, the mesenteric, renal and gonadal arteries, and ends by splitting into the two common iliac arteries.

follow.q: The abdominal aorta ends by dividing into which pair of arteries?
follow.why: At about the level of the navel the abdominal aorta splits into the right and left common iliac arteries. Each then divides into an internal iliac (pelvis) and an external iliac, which becomes the femoral artery in the thigh.

labels.name: Inferior mesenteric
labels.fn: The lowest unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta. It supplies the last part of the gut, down to the end of the tract in the pelvis.

labels.name: Common iliac
labels.fn: One of the two terminal branches of the abdominal aorta. Each splits into an internal iliac artery to the pelvis and an external iliac artery to the leg.

labels.name: Internal iliac
labels.fn: The branch of the common iliac artery that supplies the pelvic organs, the buttocks and the inner thigh.

labels.name: External iliac
labels.fn: The branch of the common iliac artery headed to the leg. It passes under the ligament in the groin and becomes the femoral artery.

labels.name: Brachial artery
labels.fn: The main artery of the upper arm, continuing from the axillary artery. It runs along the inner arm and is where blood pressure is measured with a cuff; at the elbow it splits into the radial and ulnar arteries.

follow.q: Blood pressure cuffs are placed on the upper arm because they compress which artery?
follow.why: The brachial artery runs close to the skin along the inner upper arm, at about the level of the heart, so a cuff can squeeze it shut and a stethoscope at the elbow can hear flow return.

labels.name: Radial artery
labels.fn: The forearm artery on the thumb side, from the brachial artery. At the wrist it lies just under the skin over the bone, where the radial pulse is taken.

labels.name: Femoral artery
labels.fn: The main artery of the thigh, continuing from the external iliac artery. In the groin it lies close to the skin, where the femoral pulse is felt and where catheters are often inserted.

labels.name: Popliteal artery
labels.fn: The continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee, where the popliteal pulse is felt. Below the knee it splits into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.

labels.name: Posterior tibial artery
labels.fn: The branch of the popliteal artery down the back of the leg. It passes behind the bump on the inner ankle, where its pulse is felt, and continues into the sole of the foot.

labels.name: Dorsalis pedis artery
labels.fn: The continuation of the anterior tibial artery on the top of the foot, where the pedal pulse is felt. Checking it tells you blood is reaching the end of the leg.

labels.name: Superior vena cava
labels.fn: The large vein that returns blood from the head, neck, arms and chest to the right atrium, entering it from above.

follow.q: Blood from your right arm reaches the heart through which vessel?
follow.why: Veins above the diaphragm, including those of the arms, head and neck, drain into the superior vena cava, which opens into the right atrium. The inferior vena cava drains the body below the diaphragm.

labels.name: Inferior vena cava
labels.fn: The largest vein in the body. It returns blood from everything below the diaphragm (legs, abdomen and pelvis) to the right atrium, entering it from below.

os-1-14.alt: A woman standing in anatomical position, seen from the front and slightly to one side, crossed by four flat panels. A vertical panel running front to back divides her into right and left parts (the sagittal plane). A vertical panel running side to side divides her into front and back parts (the frontal, or coronal, plane). A horizontal panel at hip level divides her into upper and lower parts (the transverse plane). A slanted panel through the lower legs is an oblique plane.

os-19-2.alt: Front view of an opened chest with the ribs cut away. The heart sits in the middle of the chest between the two lungs, resting on the dome of the diaphragm, with its pointed tip angled down and to the left. A dashed line marks the cut edge of the sac around the heart. A small side view shows the heart behind the sternum and in front of the esophagus and vertebral column.

os-19-5.alt: A small drawing of the heart with a box on its outer wall, enlarged into a slice showing the layers from inside to outside: a thin inner lining, a thick band of muscle, a thin outer covering, a narrow fluid-filled space, a thin membrane, and a tough outer fibrous layer.

os-19-6.alt: Two drawings of the outside of the heart. The front view shows the four chambers from the surface, the ear-shaped flaps of the upper chambers, the large vessels leaving the top, and surface vessels running in fat-filled grooves toward the tip. The back view shows the veins entering the upper chambers and the surface vessels on the back of the heart.

os-19-9.alt: A front view of the heart cut open in a frontal plane. It shows the two upper and two lower chambers, the wall between the lower chambers, the valves between upper and lower chambers held by thin cords to small muscles on the lower chamber walls, the valves at the exits to the two large arteries, the large veins entering, and the thick muscular wall of the lower left chamber.

os-19-12.alt: The heart seen from above with the upper chambers and large vessels removed, so all four valves are visible in one plane. Two large valves sit at the back, one with three flaps on the right side and one with two flaps on the left. Two smaller round valves with three half-moon flaps each sit in front of them.

os-19-4.alt: Two drawings of the circulation. Above, the heart with its large vessels: vessels carrying oxygen-poor blood shown in blue and vessels carrying oxygen-rich blood shown in red. Below, a loop diagram: the right side of the heart sends blood through a small loop to the capillaries of the lungs and back to the left side, which sends it through a larger loop to the capillaries of the body and back to the right side.

os-19-15.alt: Front and back views of the heart showing its own blood vessels. Red arteries branch from the base of the aorta: one runs down the front groove toward the tip, one curves around the left side in the groove between upper and lower chambers, and one runs around the right side and down the back. Blue veins run beside them and gather into a wide vein in the groove on the back of the heart that empties into the right upper chamber.

os-19-18.alt: The heart cut open in a frontal plane, seen from the front, with its conduction pathway drawn as yellow lines. A small node sits high in the wall of the right upper chamber near where the large vein from above enters. Three pathways run from it down through the right upper chamber to a second node low in the wall between the upper chambers, and a band crosses to the left upper chamber. From the second node a single bundle runs into the wall between the lower chambers, splits into right and left branches that run down toward the tip, and then fans out as fine fibers up the walls of both lower chambers.

os-20-24.alt: A front view of a standing woman with her main arteries drawn in red. The aorta rises from the heart, arches, and runs down the back of the trunk, giving branches to the head, both arms, the abdominal organs and the kidneys, then splits in the pelvis into two branches that run down each leg to the foot. The arm arteries divide at the elbow into two forearm branches that meet in arches in the palm.

os-20-25.alt: The aorta on its own. It rises from the aortic valve, where two small arteries leave for the heart muscle, curves up and over to the left, and runs straight down. Three branches leave the top of the curve: one short trunk on the right that splits in two, then separate branches to the left side of the neck and the left arm.

os-20-27.alt: The underside of the brain with its arteries in red. Two arteries rise along the front of the spinal column and join into one midline artery on the brainstem. That artery splits at its top end, and short connecting arteries link it to the two arteries arriving at the front, closing a ring of arteries around the base of the brain.

os-20-28.alt: The aorta running down the back of the chest and abdomen in front of the spine, with the ribs, diaphragm and kidneys in place. Small branches leave it in the chest for the chest wall and organs. It passes through an opening in the diaphragm, gives off a short trunk that splits three ways, single branches to the gut, paired branches to the kidneys and to the reproductive glands, and splits into two large branches in the pelvis.

os-20-11.alt: An outline drawing of a standing woman with black dots at the places where a pulse can be felt: the temple, the jaw, the side of the neck, the inner arm above the elbow, the thumb side of the wrist, the groin, the back of the knee, behind the inner ankle and on the top of the foot.

os-20-35.alt: A front view of a standing woman with her main veins drawn in blue. Veins from the head, neck and arms join into two large trunks that meet in one large vein entering the top of the heart. Veins from the legs, pelvis, kidneys and liver join a second large vein that runs up the back of the abdomen to the bottom of the heart. Superficial veins run up the inner and outer sides of each arm, and a long vein runs up the inner side of each leg.

os-20-37.alt: A side view of the head and neck showing the veins. Wide venous channels run inside the skull, along the top midline and around the back and base of the skull, and drain into a large deep vein running down the neck beside the airway. A smaller vein runs down the outside of the neck, and veins from the face and scalp join both. The neck veins end in a vein running under the collarbone.

os-20-38.alt: The veins of the right arm, front view, with deep veins shown darker than superficial ones. Deep veins run beside the forearm and arm bones. A superficial vein runs up the thumb side, another up the little-finger side, and a short vein crosses the front of the elbow to link them. All drain into a vein in the armpit and then one under the collarbone.

os-20-41.alt: The veins of the lower limb in front and back views. Deep veins run beside the leg and thigh bones and join into one vein behind the knee and one in the thigh, which passes into the pelvis. A long superficial vein runs from the inner ankle up the inner side of the leg to the groin, and a shorter one runs up the back of the calf to the back of the knee. A venous arch crosses the top of the foot.

os-20-43.alt: The abdominal organs with the veins that drain the gut. Veins from the stomach, pancreas, spleen and intestines gather into three main veins that join behind the pancreas into a single large vein running up into the liver.
